caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Cyprus has the most dramatic debt arc in this set: 59% of GDP in 2006, a low of 44.1% in 2008, then the banking crisis and bail-in pushed it to 113.6% in 2020, the series peak, with a second surge during COVID. The turnaround has been equally striking: 80.3% in 2022, projected 55.3% in 2025, driven by strong nominal growth, fiscal surpluses, and repayments. GDP grew from $20.4bn in 2006 to a projected $41.0bn in 2025. Cyprus is the poster child for post-bailout consolidation.
inflation_management: Euro membership since 2008 means the ECB sets policy; Cyprus tracked the area with sharper swings. It was 0.2% in 2009, -1.5% in 2015 during the bailout-era internal devaluation, and -1.1% in 2020. The 2022 shock pushed it to 8.1%, the series high, but disinflation was fast: 2.3% in 2024 and a projected 0.8% for 2025, one of the lowest in the euro area. The wage-indexation system (COLA) has been a recurring structural debate but did not derail the 2023-24 adjustment.

key_events.event: Joined the euro area (January 2008), gaining monetary credibility.
Banking crisis: EU-IMF bailout with the first-ever eurozone deposit bail-in (March 2013); capital controls imposed.
Exited the bailout program on schedule after a sharp but fast adjustment.
COVID-19: debt spiked to 113.6% of GDP, the series peak.
Energy shock inflation of 8.1%; rapid disinflation followed, with 2025 projected at 0.8%.

outlook_next_decade: Cyprus has earned fiscal credibility through the 2020-25 debt halving, and growth is diversified across tourism, shipping, ICT, and professional services. The risks are external: exposure to regional geopolitical shocks in the Eastern Mediterranean, and a large banking legacy that, while much reduced, still warrants caution. Inflation should remain near the ECB target; the key fiscal task is holding the gains by avoiding procyclical spending as surpluses accumulate.
